newsitem.title: UK: CE bid hinges on Northern appeal.
newsitem.headline: CE bid hinges on Northern appeal.

text.p: The fierce takeover battle for British utility Northern Electric Plc hangs on a likely appeal by Northern over a watchdog's decision to extend the bid timetable, sources close to the bid said on Sunday.

The 782 million pound ($1.3 billion) hostile offer by CE Electric, controlled by CalEnergy Co Inc, closed at 1300 GMT on Friday with the U.S. utility falling fractionally short of the number of shareholder acceptances needed to win.

But the Takeover Panel, in a dramatic move, decided late on Friday to extend the bid until 1300 GMT on Christmas Eve, apparently because Northern's brokers BZW did not initially disclose an extra 250,000 pound fee related to its performance in the bid.
A spokesman for Northern, which supplies electricity to northeast England, said its advisers would probably decide later on Sunday whether to appeal.

If they do, as seems likely, the Takeover Panel will effectively decide the fate of Northern, because CE Energy said on Saturday it had received late acceptances that tipped them over the 50 percent mark needed for victory.
"It is an extraordinary situation," said one industry source. Acceptances for the bid received by CE Electric after the orginal deadline must be approved by the Panel.
It is not yet officially known why the bid was extended, as neither the Takeover Panel nor BZW will discuss the matter until the question of an appeal is resolved.

But industry sources said newspaper reports that it was related to the fee structure had drawn a reasonable conclusion. CE Electric held 49.77 percent of the regional electricity company (Rec) at the original close -- agonisingly close but, if the Panel decides not to uphold the bid extension, a win fair and square for Northern under British takeover rules.

The U.S. energy group had complained to the takeover panel last week over buying by Northern's advisers, BZW and investment bank Schroders, of shares amounting to 2.32 percent of Northern, which it claimed was "frustrating action".
But the Panel cleared the purchases, which, though aimed at defeating the bid, are permitted under British takeover rules.

No spokesman for BZW was immediately available, but the Sunday Telegraph quoted the investment house as saying, "I can tell you...that there is no suggestion that the purchases of shares which we made in Northern to assist our client in its defence of the bid by CE Electric have been made other than fully in compliance with the law and the City code on takeovers."

However, CE Electric said in a statement on Saturday that the Panel had banned Northern's advisers from buying more shares in Northern Electric when it extended the bid deadline. A CE spokesman said on Sunday it was making no further comment.
The 650 pence-per-share bid, which was raised from 630 pence on December 6, has been hotly contested by Northern, which says the price undervalues it.
Northern had claimed it had the backing of its largest institutional investor, the Prudential, which holds around 11 percent, as well as other funds including M&G and Foreign & Colonial.
Prior to Friday's deadline, CE Electric already held 30 percent of Northern, bought on the open market.
On Saturday it claimed to own or have acceptances for shares totalling 50.03 percent of Northern, with additional late acceptances still being counted.

Northern is the only one of the original 12 cash-rich Recs to have successfully fought off a takeover bid, spending 560 million pounds on shareholder benefits to fend off Trafalgar House, now part of Norway's Kvaerner, last year.
Nine of the 12 Recs privatised in 1990 have been sold or agreed to takeovers since they came up for grabs when the government's protective golden share expired in March 1995.
If CE Electric wins control of Northern, only two of the original 12 Recs will remain independent -- Yorkshire Electricity and Southern Electric. ($1=.6002 Pound)
